utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand you wish to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, very briefly. Since the winter recess is about to begin, as you know full well, I wanted to ask you to make it possible for me to take advantage of this recess so that I could go to Moscow to the Bakulev Scientific Institute of academician Professor Bockeria for health reasons. See far I've been examined by two experts from that institute, and I have full trust in this institute. It is the top-notch medical institution in Russia. It would not affect your programme in any way, because I would be back here again before this is resumed in accordance with your programme, so I'm asking you to make this possible for me for health reasons. I don't see any hindrance in the way of this because it really would not disturb your programme in any way. So that would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've been fairly flexible in relation to the presentation of motions by you orally because the Rules allow for it and there is an advantage to be gained by an oral submission in certain circumstances, but this is, in effect, an application for provisional release, which should be made in writing, and you -- I think you very well know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that what I say here and what is recorded in the transcript has the same effect as any written submission would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if we are to even begin to consider this application, there's a host of matters that you'd have to attend to antecedent to our consideration of it. For one, we'd need a medical report in relation to the particular condition that affects you and which you say can be treated adequately in Moscow. Secondly, it's an application for provisional release, which would have to be covered by adequate guarantees. None of that you have presented. So I can't believe that you are serious in making this presentation. I advise that you consult Mr. Kay as to how to put in a proper application, and we'll consider it. Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also have a matter to raise in private session, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber has the new formulation of these documents, it will see that the English translations come at the beginning in two sections, I think divided by a green page. So the first section is for the first notebook and the second for the second, obviously enough. The page numbers of the notebooks are at the top left-hand side of each page. There's a separate serial number at the bottom of the centre of the page which is simply for convenience purposes, but one way or another we should be able to find our way through the material quickly. The relevant parts of the notebooks have been identified by oblong markings surrounding the passage in which we have a particular interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, do you have the full notebook in front you, copies of the notebooks in front of you, coming your way?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice, I haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's coming there now. And if Mr. Prendergast would always lay the English page on the overhead projector when I ask him to but not on all occasions because sometimes I will not. And if you, Mr. Sel, could start with the first of your notebooks. You will have to turn them round that way. Before I ask you the first question, just help me with this: Do you accept that there was any crime committed by soldiers of your unit in the course of the period January to June of 1999? Any serious crime committed by soldiers of your unit?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldiers, Mr. Nice, did not commit a single serious crime that would be condemned by the unit and that would require the initiation of court proceedings against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Would you go, please, to page 4 of your first document; your first notebook, and we see outlined then a reference to a man called Misel Seregi. Probably that's the way it reads. Does that change your thinking at all about the question I gave you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Misel Sergei was my soldier until February 1999. In mid-February 1999 I handed over this unit to another officer and I received a new unit, so it was until then that he was my soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... man trained by you, was it then, or looked after by you for long enough?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until February 1999, mid-February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to page of your diary, page 48, and if the Chamber goes to page 13 at the bottom middle to find it, we can see again at the bottom, listed with a lot of other soldiers, Sergei Misel. So he's there again. And you know why I'm asking you the questions about this man, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this, Mr. Nice. This is the 30th of July, 1998. This is a list of men who went out on mission to provide in-depth security of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to remind the Chamber, if we go on to page 71 of your documents, page 28 at the bottom in the English but page 71 of your documents, you see the name of another person of interest in relation to the question of commission of crimes: Lieutenant Rade Radojevic?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, the same thing. Rade Radojevic was there until mid-February 1999, so I was no longer his commanding officer after handing over this particular duty in mid-February 1999. Practically all soldiers and officers were then placed under the command of a new company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go on to page 31 in the English, date -- or page 89 of your document, page 31 - I'm going to use the bottom numbers for the Chamber, it's probably quicker - we see that you had a patrol in the Kusnin Grcin area. Kusnin in your area of responsibility, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 34 in the English, page 110 of your document. Again we see reference to Kusnin. That will do for the time being because you know --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I just explain something to you. My unit was in that area. That's when I was the commander of that unit. It was providing in-depth security of the state border, and it is logical that it used patrols to secure the state border. So until the 15th of February I was commander of that unit in that area. From the 15th of February onwards I was transferred to another unit, another area, and I received this new unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tesic was another soldier in your unit at one time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Another one of my former soldiers who was under my command until the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, Lieutenant Colonel Mancic is a person who features. We can see him in your diary, I think, in your notebook in due course. Just explain the position: Mancic was the security representative in your unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. At that time he was not in my unit at all. When I left that unit, he came. Only later, that is; March 1999. That is to say that I was no longer in that unit when he came. So I personally do not know the man and I never saw him, because the area of that unit was about 20 kilometres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Never saw Mancic at all?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know, and we'll just remind the Chamber of this, that the four men, Mancic, Radojevic, Sergei, and Tesic, were one example - almost the only example - of people tried for war crimes and they were tried in respect of an offence committed at Kusnin, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Nice, when that crime was committed, but I do know that they were convicted and that they're serving their sentences in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know, and we're going to look at the transcript of the trial which we have in due course, but you'll know this in any event, that the only reason there was a trial for war crimes of these people was because the young soldier Tesic gave himself up. He reported himself for what he'd been made to do by officers above him. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know something about that, Mr. Nice, but I don't know at all about Tesic reporting these officers and that comrade of his. I don't know what that was all about. I know that proceedings were there against them and that they were convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you know that this act of probably perceived disloyalty to the VJ by Tesic only led to a trial after this accused was surrendered to this Tribunal. There was no trial in 1999 or 2000, was there? Those men were only tried after this accused was surrendered to this Tribunal. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who carried out proceedings and how, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, assuming time allows, in a little more detail later. My next questions, with the Court's leave, should be done in closed session, please. It's the matter that I was given leave to deal with last week in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on to new matters, particularly new matters, remember last week I was asking you in general terms about activity in the Babaj Boks area, and I was asking you about offences involving rape there. Is it right that offences of rape were committed in that area, to your certain knowledge and at your instructions?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first let's get one thing straight: Soldiers B and D were not my soldiers, and please doesn't mention them to me again. Soldiers A and C left the unit in June 1998. That means they left the encampment where they were undergoing regular training. So these soldiers did not take part in any combat activity or any operation in that place, nor were there any rapes in that period or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In general throughout the period 1998 and 1999, there were attacks on civilians in their houses and in their villages under a policy whereby many of them were killed at your decision. That's the correct position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm telling you again this is completely untrue. I don't know how you got that statement from those soldiers. Even the way you took it is subject to dispute. Soldiers, when they are in a camp, cannot leave it of their own will. They can go in an organised manner for medical check-ups, they return in an organised way, and in the same organised way they go out for training. And there was nothing of the kind in Babaj Boks, because we were not in Babaj Boks but in the area of Sulane, where we had regular training. The picture you're trying to paint is completely inappropriate, because it's untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the overhead projector, or I think it fits on the overhead projector, and I'm not sure, has it been given an exhibit number? Not exhibited yet. May it have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To remind the Chamber, in the area we've just speaking about is to the south-west of Djakovica, I'm now turning to the area north of Djakovica near the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the lake there, Radonjicko Lake, we see to the west Gornji Bites. You say you never went to the lake yourself, Mr. Sel, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never been in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in charge, then, of the soldiers at the lake?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, sometime in August, pursuant to orders from the battalion command, one of my platoons was engaged in securing the dam on the reservoir. The commander was Radojevic Rade, who was commanding a battalion of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long was he there for altogether?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of killings at Gornja Bites of men and women and teenage children?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, Mr. Nice. I know that the military police battalion undertook combat operations against terrorists who were located above the Radonjicko Lake or reservoir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if there were combat operations in 1998, still peacetime, and if those combat operations led to deaths, they would have been recorded, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the rule of service and the legislation stipulates how the army is used in peacetime. I don't see anything strange about that. All the regulations say that the army is used against terrorists, not against unarmed civilians, women, or children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, please, if you didn't understand the question the last time, if there were combat operations in 1998 and if in the course of those operations people were killed, where do we turn to find the records of the deaths and of how the deaths were investigated? Because we haven't found the documents yet despite every effort. Where?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that was an area in the -- or, rather, outside the area of responsibility of my unit so I don't know about it. I can't tell you anything because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You sent Lieutenant Rade Radojevic, subsequently to be convicted of murder, as we know, you sent him up there. Did he report back to you? Did he provide daily reporting records of these combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have to distinguish between providing security to special-purpose installations and combat against terrorists. This platoon went to secure the dam, not to engage in combat with terrorists, and that soldier was not engaged in combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can take that no further. I'll move on swiftly to see if there's anything else I want to cover from the general topics I was exploring last week. Now let's move to something rather different. The topics I'm now going to raise with you come from Soldier C, and as you know, you're to say nothing in open session that might identify this person. Do you understand that, Mr. Sel?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this soldier, and you know his identity because that's been dealt with in private session and you realise you must never reveal that to anyone outside this room, but you know him and you know something of the circumstances of his joining and leaving your unit. I must suggest to you, coming from him, that you operated a policy where civilians were killed pretty well at will in the course of ambushes and similar operations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are at cross-purposes or we totally misunderstand each other or you know nothing about military matters. This has nothing to do with murdering civilians. If you think a civilian is somebody who carries 20 rifles, machine-guns, mortars, and ammunition and opens fire at my soldiers, if you still consider them to be a civilian, then please stand up against them. I would like to see you defending yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The suggestion I'm putting to you is that in what was nominally peacetime, you sent out units on a regular basis to ambush, in the middle of the night, any Albanian you could find moving, especially if they were moving towards or from the border, regardless of whether they were armed, regardless of whether they were men intending to fight. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely untrue. That is something you made up. Everyone knows what an ambush is meant for. I'm telling you again, you know nothing about military matters and that's why you can't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, you must carry on being offensive if you think it's helpful or if it's what you've been advised to do, but please answer the questions. In peacetime, why is an ambush an appropriate way of dealing with people who may be entirely innocent?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm telling you again you do not know anything about military matters. I don't want to take an insulting tone, unlike you. An ambush is simply meant to stop -- to stop anyone who is moving unlawfully in the border belt. Now, tell me, what could armed civilians be doing when they cross over the state border in an inappropriate place, from Albania, carrying weapons? If you think they're going for a walk or going shopping, it's your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had a policy as well of getting -- of getting Muslims to kill incoming Muslims wherever you could, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Nice. In my eyes, every soldier is just a soldier, regardless of ethnicity, faith, or anything else. He is a soldier as long as he is in the army and as long as he is under oath, and we never discriminated on any grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, did you mean that question, a policy of getting Muslims to kill incoming Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incoming Albanians, yes, I did. Albanians, yes. Albanians rather than Muslims. Getting Muslims to kill Albanians coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did nothing, did you, in your unit, or so far as you know in the others, to alert soldiers to their duties under the Geneva Conventions, either at this time in 1998 or when war was declared; is that right? Not war was declared, after a state of emergency was declared.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is completely untrue. All soldiers were familiar with the rule of conduct for the armed force. Every soldier knew what he is allowed to do and what he isn't allowed to do. They carried this booklet with them, and every unit commander was familiar with the fundamental rules of military law, and we abided by the Geneva Conventions whereas the terrorists didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was simply -- not even -- I must suggest to you not even a pretense at applying or teaching your soldiers about the Geneva Conventions until after the young soldier Tesic reported himself for the killing that he had been made to do in April 1999; isn't that right? It was only when he turned himself in so that you could no longer be as lawless as you had been that people started saying something about the duties in war; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You realise we're going to look, assuming I get time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. That's completely incorrect. Soldiers were trained for their job, for their duty. Everybody knows what the role of the army in peacetime is. It was not engaged in any unlawful activities. If there were individual violations, perpetrators were prosecuted in a timely manner. All soldiers were familiar with their obligations and duty, and I'm telling you again, every soldier had this rule with them and they were read a lecture on the Geneva Conventions and international --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- law of war. Just a minute. In every combat order great attention was paid to underline respect for civilians, conservation of property, and the rule that fire must not be opened at anyone before fire is opened at you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at the list of names, remembering that you must say nothing to identify them. There was an occasion in June of 1998 when Soldier A and Soldier C were ordered by you to go and kill a farmer tending his cow. Do you remember that little detail?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's not true at all. First of all, I don't know what all this is about; and secondly, where the army is, it is common knowledge how far civilians can come up close. So there was no need to open fire on any civilian just to issue a caution to say that they had approached the camp, which they were not supposed to do, not to kill civilians. That is your arbitrary conclusion or an attempt on these two men to gain something by making a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the only reason that they were able to let this man live was because they weren't surrounded by or in close proximity to Serb soldiers, because if Serb soldiers had been around, they would have known that the pressure on them was so great they could hardly resist your order. On this occasion, the man with the cow escaped. Think back. Are you really suggesting that this detail's been entirely created or does it have some connection to something you can remember, Mr. Sel?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it is entirely created.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my unit, that is to say the number of soldiers I had - please allow me to finish - there were not only Serbs, there were Hungarians, Romanians, Czechs as well, and other ethnic groups in addition to Muslims. So that was the strength of my men. It was a multinational unit, not a purely single ethnic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Keep your eyes on Soldier C, please, on the list. When he first joined your unit, you gave instructions how to behave, and in the course of giving those instructions, which were instructions how to kill, you announced that you had yourself killed a six-month-old baby, taking it from its mother's arms. Do you remember saying something about that to a group including Soldier C? Do you find that amusing?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please stop making these fabrications. All this is a farce that has been made up and stories told. It's not correct at all. I'm a professional soldier. I'm a professional soldier, and my attitude to my profession is professional. I'm not a criminal. I'm not a killer or murderer of women or children or anybody else. I carried out my duties professionally, Mr. Nice, and everything that you're trying to do now is just a concocted story.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1998 is still a time of apparent peace. Can you show us, please, the records of what happened to the people who, in the ambushes near the border, died? Can you show us the records if your operation was so lawful?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while my unit was providing in-depth security for the state border, there was no intervention on its part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You dug a big pit, didn't you, on Morina Mount, and that's where some of the bodies were buried. Did you bury bodies at Morina Mount?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, my unit wasn't in the area of Morina at all. It was at Sulane, Rogasca, where it was engaged in training. Now, Morina and the watchtowers there and Kosare is quite another area altogether and comes under the responsibility of quite another unit. I was never in the area myself nor any of my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When villages were entered and when people were killed, booty was obtained. What happened to it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't understand that question of yours. What booty? War booty is the weapons you come across that are seized from other people; parts of uniforms, communications devices, and anything else that these people carried with them. There was no other war booty and we never entered inhabited areas to kill civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, the product of plunder --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me, was there a special policy in relation to cameras, that cameras were always set on one side for fear of the soldiers using them to photograph events that would reveal the crimes that were being committed? Were cameras always set on one side, and or is that detail, suggested to us by the people to whom we've spoken, simply a fabrication?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't want to read from -- out from the rules of service, but soldiers doing their military service are prohibited from having on them cameras or anything else that records in video fashion. So please refrain your questions to what refers to my unit. I can't give you answers to other questions concerning other units, just concerning my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, look, please, at Soldier D. You say he wasn't in your unit, he was in somebody else's unit, but the propositions coming concern you and I'd like you to deal with them. This soldier was there until the agreements in the summer of 1999 that will led to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say that this Soldier D was in some other unit. All he said that he wasn't in his own unit. Now, whether such a soldier exists or does not exist, he cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about Rambo, please. Who was Rambo?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Rambo is. Rambo, if you think -- if you're thinking about Sylvester Stallone, then perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Rambo is a nom de guerre, a pseudonym. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know any such commanding officer. And we don't call each other by our nicknames but by our rank, first name and last name. And it is strictly prohibited to assign nicknames or to call each other on the basis of nicknames. We address each other on the basis of rank, name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that in 1998 the area of Smonica, which we can see on the map - I'll just find it - was an area of particular difficulty for you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, from the period of May up until August 1998 along the Djakovica-Ponosevac road, there were about 20 soldiers who were seriously wounded, and Smonica was the strongest terrorist stronghold.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was that -- so my suggestion is right; it was a place of great difficulty. Is it right that it was so difficult for you that people were killed indiscriminately; men, women and children? Is that what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you recall when the first statement was given when you asked me a similar question, all civilians, because of pressure from the terrorists, Smonica, Donje Nec, that general area, Ramoc, left their places and went to Djakovica. And those villages were organised for defence and it was only the terrorists that were in the villages. There were no civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The information presented to the Prosecution includes that, far from there being KLA people for you to attack in these villages, the KLA typically withdrew ahead of the army's, the VJ's arrival, and all that was left was civilians who were at random killed and sometimes allowed to go. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true at all. Explain to me who dug the trenches, the communicating trenches, dugouts, shelters, firepower positions for mortars and machine-guns? Who brought in all that weaponry and left the anti-armoured mines along the roads? This is something that the villagers did, this is something that the terrorists did who tried to do certain things that they weren't supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Soldier D, there from -- right through to the end again says, "No instruction about the Geneva Convention." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's not true at all. First of all, if the soldier exists in a unit with the officer we mentioned, then he was at the 120-millimetre mortars, which means two kilometres away from that area to three kilometres away. He never entered that area nor did he see what there was there. And I and my soldiers crossed that entire area on foot, as opposed to him, and saw what there was there. I'd like you to have been with me. Then I'd see what story you'd be telling now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your answer. It must be my mistake. I asked you whether he'd been instructed about the Geneva Convention and you said, "If the soldier exists in a unit with the officer we mentioned, then he was two kilometres away from the area." From what area?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I repeat, you don't seem to understand military matters. 120-millimetre mortars are for fire power support, which means that they target at a distance, as opposed to a motorised company which takes part in the fighting directly. So that's where the difference lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pursue whichever policy you find helpful so far as your attitude to me and the Court is concerned, but I still come back to my question. I asked you about the Geneva Convention and you replied with an observation about Soldier C being two kilometres away from "that area." Well, what area; and what was there for him to see in that area that's relevant to the Geneva Conventions? The random killing you were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to tell you again: All the soldiers to the very last soldier working as a cook are well acquainted with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, and each soldier had with him a booklet of conduct of soldiers in war and laws governing war. So regardless of the fact whether they were in rifle units, motorised units or reinforcement units, they were all well acquainted with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. And before they went on assignment, attention was strictly drawn to the soldiers about their conduct toward civilians, behaviour toward civilians, to cease fire in case of encountering unarmed civilians, and a general respect for an armed -- a wounded adversary. And if I said that he was at a distance of two kilometres, that means that when we cleared up the terrorist stronghold of Smonica, the firepower position was two kilometres behind us from which we were given support, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there wasn't anything that could have been going on without us seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness D, not Witness C; my slip. Can you explain, please, how it might be that Witness D says he saw soldiers with red berets and apparently being Red Berets in your general area? Were they there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the army of Yugoslavia you have a number of different berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every special -- well, not special, but every unit. Then you have reconnaissance men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help me with this and we'll move on. Were special units coming from, say, Belgrade as part of a Red Beret unit or not?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not aware of that, because where my unit was active they were not there, so I can't tell you something I don't know about, that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. In the transcript there is no mention of what the witness said, so I suppose there was no translation. He said that the red berets were born by reconnaissance men, scouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There wasn't a problem with head gear, was there, whereby you all had to get new head gear and got red berets, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is just not true. I repeat again -- you switched my microphone off now. You just switched my microphone off now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no control over your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please have the microphone switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then somebody else does. Mr. Nice, I repeat again: The motorised unit, infantry units, those linked to the equipment, had grey berets. The scouts had red berets, and military police units had black berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... incidentally, for us how using mortars in peacetime where the mortar lands a couple of kilometres away is other than indiscriminate use of force? How can it be so targeted as to ensure it hits only the KLA and not the civilians? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I repeat again: In the area where there was combat, there were no civilians. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is a peacetime -- this is a --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to finish. We have our reconnaissance men, our scouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is peacetime, isn't it. No state of emergency, civilians living there, tending their cattle, and you can send mortars in peacetime a couple of kilometres away at a village. Is that what you used to do?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're not understanding military matters again. That is the legal use of the army in peacetime, in an anti-terrorist struggle. So the terrorists have the right to kill our soldiers and commanding officers, do they, to wound and maim them, and we don't have the right to defend ourselves, is that it? We never opened fire first ourselves. And secondly, when we did open fire, we strictly saw that we opened fire at targets where the shooting was coming from, because we have our observers, we have our calculators who provide us with the necessary data for our firing not on civilians but strictly at firepower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far, moving up until the end of March 1999, you've provided me with no answers to the general question where can we find a -- a listing of the people who were killed, where were they buried, how were they taken away. Just confirm to me that you're unable to help with any of those details for the period up and until the end of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the area where combat operations were taking place, where my unit was engaged in anti-terrorist struggles, we did not come across a single killed or wounded terrorist. We found the traces of blood and traces of people being dragged across the earth, but we didn't actually find any wounded or killed terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I assume that the terrorists who survived pulled them out and took them elsewhere. What they did with them, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the second half of April of 1999, the problem with the bodies that you were killing, or the people you were killing was becoming more problematic, and is it right that all units, that's Soldier D's unit but also your unit, were making use of the Obilic electric plant to the West of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's not correct at all. There were no civilians nor was there any killing or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What isn't true about my suggestion about the Obilic plant?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Obilic electric plant performed its function. What else was going on there I don't know, it was far away from me, but what you're thinking about, none of that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just what am I thinking about?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we could not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What am I thinking about, Mr. Sel?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, you want to ascribe to me certain crimes that were taking place in the area which never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, to ascribe it to my unit and to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What am I suggesting to you about the Obilic electricity plant, please? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you mentioned the Obilic thermoelectric power plant; I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You seem to understand the suggestion I'm making. Let me make it clear: The Obilic plant was used by the soldiers to burn and destroy the bodies of the people they'd killed, wasn't it, and you knew that because you were one of the officers involved in it.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if Soldier D describes this as a general practice applicable to all units at that time, he's completely made it up, has he? A detail as precise as that, completely made it up?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's just not true. It's pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Deva border checkpoint, was that within your general area of operation or not?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I held positions from Maja Kraljica to Cafa Vanez, which means there was no checkpoint in the Deva region, because the watchtower was hit by a NATO airstrike and there was no road leading up to it. So I don't know what checkpoint you're thinking of. It's a slope at an altitude of about 1.000 metres, which means it's a mountain, and there was the area of defence of my unit up there, above the watchtower, and there was no checkpoint at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there Albanians in that area, seeking to -- I beg your pardon, were there Kosovo Albanians in that area, seeking from time to time to get across to Albania?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. When I arrived on the 5th of April, on the basis of the reports by my subordinates and the deployment of the units, we established that there were no civilians where my unit was deployed. What happened before my unit arrived, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before your unit, might it have been Elifat Feta who was in charge of that particular area?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. In the area there was just the border unit which came under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 24th of March --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he was elsewhere. Where he was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you present when Vukovic, as it were, rallied the troops at the start of the NATO aggression, as it's described, on the 24th of March? Were you present when he did that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there was an order for anti-terrorist struggle which we received in the evening, so it was only us company commanders who received this order for an anti-terrorist struggle, not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Soldier D says that at that time Vukovic told him and others that the Albanians had to be driven from Kosovo and there should not be even an Albanian ear left in Kosovo. Can you think of some troop-rallying phrase by Vukovic that might have been remembered as that, or do you say that that's completely made up?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me repeat again: The order for an anti-terrorist struggle was issued to us company commanders. He was not able to address the units because there were NATO airstrikes going on at the time. In the Djakovica barracks, all the units were at their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to go through the diary now, and, Your Honours, if I use the English page number for the Court and the -- systematically, and the diary page number for the witness, it will probably enable us to go through as swiftly as is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I do, one other detail: As to a 60-millimetre -- as to a mortar, is it right that it destroys pretty well everything within a 60-metre radius?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you go, please, to English page 7, your page 35. Not on the overhead projector. Yes, not on the overhead projector. You see part of the way down part 35, 14 people at the lake. Would that be the lake we've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourteen soldiers with Lieutenant Radojevic that went up there to secure the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further on down that page, immediately under the name Sergei, you see a reference to the name Sipka. It's all in your hand. Is that Milan Sipka?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. Those are ways in which we differentiate between them. It says Sipka Sulane. They are indicators and distinctions. You have distinct points which end with the guards in order to have them perform their duties, so they are distinction signs, which all armies in the world use these distinction signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It actually reads, does it not, Sipka something Sulane?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sulane, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you always have the same starting letter. The second word needs to start with the same letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is the estimate for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My intention is to finish by the end of the next session. I have to do one exercise with this book and I have to do an exercise with something else. It may be less. Can we go on, please, to page 11 in the English, the 12th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is lay an ambush above Mazrek towards Sisman Boks. There's one indication in your documents to the fact that you were indeed ambushing people. You weren't arresting them and taking them prisoner, were you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was that English page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 11, I'm so sorry. 11 in the English, 45 in the diary -- in the whatever it's called, the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Lay an ambush above Mazrek towards Sisman Boks."

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this ambush above Mazrek towards Sisman Boks ensured communication towards Smonica. That is to say Djakovica, Ponosevac, Junik, that general line or road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did we ever get a record of what actually happened in one of these ambushes; how many people were killed, whether any prisoners were taken? We don't, do we?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me repeat again: Had anything happened, had there been any combat, it would certainly have been written down in the report to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't got those, you see, and I want to know what happened in peacetime in these ambushes. Let's go over, please, to English page 12, your page 47, and again it's a very rapid reference. We can see "3 more going to the lake tomorrow." The lake had quite a lot of your attention, didn't it, sending people there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have soldiers up there, so it's one set of soldiers taking the place of the other soldiers. There are 14 soldiers. If three go on furlough, you have to fill up that number and bring it up to strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 13 in English, 30th of July 1998, top entry, "ambush going according to plan." But we still don't know what the product of the ambush was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't say "ambush going according to plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, it says, "according to plan." Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How should we read that, Mr. Sel: "Ambush according to plan"? What does that mean, on page 48?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that regular security is being maintained and that somebody has been sent up to the Jasevica-Ponosevac-Junik road in the region we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it's still --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And let me repeat again: Had there been any combat, then certainly that would have been recorded in the report going up to the brigade command or, rather, my report would have gone up the line and then further up the chain onwards. Since that did not happen, then there was no report to send of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you really saying that all these ambushes that we've seen and we're going to see perhaps more of actually led to nothing happening? Nobody died, nobody captured; nothing?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the totality of 1998, nothing happened in Babaj Boks at all. You just laid ambushes and never saw a soul. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the unit was not at Babaj Boks, it was in Sulane. Sulane is above Babaj Boks and that is a different place. We were just carrying out our regular duties. At least, my unit did not clash with armed terrorists who were carrying weapons but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in other places there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, what persons were the object of this, of the ambushes that were laid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the aim of that ambush was to prevent armed smuggling from the Republic of Albania into the territory of Kosovo, thus arming terrorists. So these ambushes were not placed in order to capture civilians but to prevent smuggling arms from the territory of the Republic of Albania in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take the 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. I'm bound to say for myself I'm not finding this exercise very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry to hear that. I'll try and make it more helpful because I think a full exploration of this book will be of great assistance in the arguments the Prosecution is going to make. But to save time, let's deal with it in this way, just to get through a few pages: You will find references to ambushes again on English pages 19, 20 and 22, which is pages 59 and 60 of the original. We will move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one general question, or one proposition. It's true, isn't it, Mr. Sel, that your troops acted frequently in a state of drunkenness, aided by drugs, and it was necessary to have them in that state to get them to do the things that you needed them to do.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's not correct at all. What you're saying is quite arbitrary. It is strictly forbidden to drink while on duty in the military, and also the use of narcotics is prohibited, so all of that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let's go to page 62 of your document, page 23 in the English. Still in 1998. Perhaps you'd like to explain these entries to us. First of all, it refers to tying-up cord being taken along. Then at 0800 hours, it refers to a mobile radio, and then it says this: "Civilians --" well, you read it out to us in case it's been translated in a way that you're not happy with. Fourth line down, "civilna lica --" go on, read it out.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it says here: "The said persons who do not have documents, do not have legal documents issued by the MUP, that is to say IDs and residence permits, in the area should be arrested and brought in." And, of course, handed over to the security organs or, rather, the MUP organs that are in charge. Because there were quite a few persons hiding in the houses of civilians who had proper documents and whose residence was properly registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please just read the language that's actually on page 62. Read it slowly and the interpreters will translate it for us. All right? "Civilna lica ..." and so on. You read it.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Nice: "Civilian persons who do not have documents should be arrested and tied up." That means handed over to the organs in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not what you said the time before. You didn't say tied up. Help us. What does "tied up" mean? Hmm? It's in your book.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, at that time our units had the same kind of powers like the MUP unit. That is to say all persons who do not have documents and who are in the border belt, that means that they came from the Republic of Albania, so it was our duty to arrest them, tie them, and hand them over to the appropriate authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Sel, which version do you want us to go away with? You've tried two. Were you or were you not tying up the civilians with rope?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the tasks. However, we didn't find anyone without documents so we didn't have to tie anyone, arrest anyone, or bring anyone in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the first time you read that passage out you omitted the passage about tying up. You put it in another way. What are you doing in peacetime tying up civilians with rope? Hmm? And this one can go on the overhead projector, please, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, obviously you don't understand me. This was an order. If one came across such persons who do not have residence permits for the border belt, that means automatically that that person was not from there, that that person was hiding in there, did not have valid documents. So we were duty-bound to arrest these persons, tie them, and bring them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was possible that these persons were armed or that they had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- hand grenades, so we had to take measures with a view to preventing that kind of thing from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I don't have time to explore all these questions or, as one of the learned Judges once said, to batten -- tie them all down or knock them all down. Down the page, Munja. We all heard about Munja. It's a famous paramilitary group. What is Munja doing in your handwriting in this book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page is that, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Munja. Extensive reference to Munja in "Under Orders." We've looked at it; photographs, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 23 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you've misunderstood this. Munja is the first reserve frequency of channel 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it has nothing to do with any paramilitary organisation. It's only the members of the army who were there. Munja is the first reserve frequency --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on channel 500. That is a normal code. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the fact that it overlaps with something else ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over on the left-hand side we've got Karlo 118, Jovica 121. Four lines down we've got Sel 110, and then we've got Rambo 120. You denied knowing anything about Rambo, so perhaps you'd like to explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Possibly this was an abbreviation of the name and surname of the officer involved. Well, it's not that strange. There were persons, officers who had that kind of names; Rambo, Tarzan, Bruce Lee. I was not their godfather, I wasn't giving them their names. These are the names of officers who were engaged in this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us it was forbidden to have nicknames, you told us you didn't know who Rambo was, and here he is. Just perhaps you'd like to tell us now what his name is.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's a normal name. I wasn't his godfather, it wasn't I who decided what his name would be. It's a name like any other name given to a child when a child is born or, rather, the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, it's obvious, isn't it, that these people on the left-hand side, including you, are people with forces at your command. You've got 110, by the looks of things, unless I'm wrong, or maybe it's a radio frequency, I don't know, but these are commanding officers of some kind or another. You didn't know who Rambo was, now you do. What's his first name, Rambo? Is it Rambo Rambo or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that. I don't remember that. But these are the names of all the officers who were on the unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in order to maintain communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- bottom of the page, same page, but for you it's page 63, top of page 63, please, Mr. Sel. "Zylfaj Prusa" cleansing or cleaning. What does it mean? Prusa is a place, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, these are abandoned border posts, our summer border posts that became the headquarters of the terrorists. When terrorists came from the Republic of Albania to our territory, that is what they used. And as for cleaning, cleansing, I've explained it several times here but if you don't understand, I will read out yet again what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So cleansing has to do with moving people about, does it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the regulation of a platoon in a mountainous -- in a mountain unit is very clear, and I've already read it out and I thought that it was perfectly clear what cleaning meant; cleaning the terrain from remnants of terrorist groups. That is a shortened version, but if you wish, I'm going to read out from the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What we know is that Prusa was being cleansed, whatever is meant by that, on this particular day, yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat yet again, Mr. Nice: Zulfaj and Prusa are abandoned summer border posts that the terrorists used as their strongholds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on, Witness D identified, without any access to any material, Rambo as the person who was in charge of the business of moving bodies to -- I'll come back to Rambo in a minute. We'll move on. Just over the page, please, English page 24, still on your page 63, there's a second reference to Munja, beside Reserve 540; Munja. Did you know about the Munja paramilitary group? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is a reserve channel, code Munja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn to English page 26, your page 66. Now, you'll see in page 66 - I'm not sure whether it's been highlighted - a reference to Pusto Selo. We can see it halfway down our page. Is Pusto Selo in your general area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it -- and it stayed within the general area of responsibility of your unit right through until the end of hostilities in June of 1999. It's right, isn't it, that Pusto Selo, although it's not charged in this indictment, was the location of a --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, sorry. It's not correct. In 1998, on the 2nd of August, anti-terrorist action took place in that area and these are excerpts from the assignment that I got from the battalion commander, so if you carefully had all of this translated, that's what it says: The line of anti-terrorist fighting, terrorists noticed, about 300 men, also what they had; sniper rifles, recoilless guns, machine-guns, bunkers, shelters, and they are on that line. The KLA headquarters is in the village of Vranjak, so this is information about the enemy or, rather, terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, just as the Obilic power station, you understood the allegation before it was made. Pusto Selo in March 1999 was the subject of a massacre of a hundred civilians, wasn't it? It was in your area of responsibility. Do you know how they died?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, in that period our unit was not in that place at all. We explained very nicely that the anti-terrorist action started on the 25th and we explained where it was actually taking place; along the axis of Bela Crkva, Brestovac, Mala Hoca, Randubrava, Retimlje, Neprebiste, Mamusa. There is no mention of Pusto Selo. Pusto Selo is on the other side completely. It is outside the area of responsibility of our unit, and this is the year 1998, the 2nd of September. So if you take all of this into account, please have a look at the map and you will see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask my questions so we'll have the answer. Page 27 in the English, page 68 for you. The setting on fire of the stacks, fences, and then something about the houses and a word illegible. You might be able to read the word yourself on page 68. You can see it on the original at the bottom left-hand side of 68. "Kuca" something. So what does that mean? "Setting on fire of the stacks, fences; houses" something.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, if you read my notebook that carefully, you could have read the following: "The setting on fire of stacks, fences, and houses, no." So this was just a form of jotting down what was said. So it was not allowed, the random setting on fire of haystacks, fences and houses. Don't laugh, Mr. Nice. Read it carefully. It says "ne"; "no." I know what you want, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We thought it might have said Nay but the translators weren't prepared to say Nay. So if you read it rather more carefully, it actually says, "The setting on fire of stacks, fences; houses, no." Now, then, what are you doing writing in your book anything about the setting on fire --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to me. What are you doing in your book saying anything about the setting on fire of haystacks unless it was happening?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's not a semicolon, it's the letter I. So it means "and." So it's a continuation of the sentence. That is one of the measures that is communicated to the soldiers before going out on mission. So what I've said is most strictly prohibited. They are not allowed to do any such thing. If they do it, then they will have disciplinary measures taken against them. I think that you will understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what pattern of setting on fire haystacks, fences and houses had there been that led to it being necessary to give this instruction, please?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there was no pattern and there was no order. This is one of my measures regarding the soldiers. That was something that the soldiers were not supposed to do. And they were not allowed to violate this rule. So it is not possible that they did things like that because that would not look like things that soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia did. That was not our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, they weren't supposed to slaughter. They weren't supposed to rape, were they?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, again you're presenting these arbitrary facts. Soldiers were not slaughtering or killing innocent civilians. Please don't go on about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, it is a good question. Why would you specifically give such orders about something that is so obvious that any soldier wouldn't need to be told about it? Now, that would suggest it had been happening and they needed to be reminded. That's the question you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, this is my own statement. This is what I am conveying to the soldiers by way of my order. I'm not allowing them to do things that are impermissible and that do not pertain to the work of soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia. So that is the way I protect the buildings there and the population, if there was any population left there. So the point was that that kind of thing was banned. I did not allow soldiers to do that. This is my measure prohibiting things that are not permissible. So if -- any kind of violence, any kind of torching of property, destruction of property is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the very point you've just made: It doesn't say any form of violence is prohibited. You've been very selective in what you've said and that's why you're being asked the question. You haven't said, for example, "You mustn't slaughter civilians," and I'm curious as to why you've chosen these particular items to include in an order when they're out of line, obviously, with all the stuff that goes before on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you wish to answer His Honour?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bonomy, this is a work notebook where I enter my own obligations vis-a-vis the superior command and vis-a-vis my subordinates. This is one of the security measures, and it is well known what soldiers, members of the units, are supposed to do vis-a-vis civilians as opposed to armed terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've tried to put the generality of the allegations made against you by Witnesses A, B, C -- by Soldiers A, B, C and D, but I should just add this detail: Coming again without access to your documents or anything else from Soldier C - and you can remind yourself Soldier C only 1998, as you would say, longer period otherwise - he says that people were -- that soldiers used gas bombs, or it may be gas, in the houses to disable the inhabitants. The soldiers went in and plundered everything and then set the houses on fire, destroying the corpses in the process. Now, that's the allegation that's included in the allegations made against you throughout 1998 and 1999. Is there truth in that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there is not the tiniest bit of truth in that. I've already said that these were statements made to your associates a year later in order for these soldiers to get some benefits. They were in the unit for five days, regular training, on the camp premises. They did not take part in any kind of combat action. When they left the unit, they never came back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at just a few more entries in your diaries to see what's there and what is not. Page 40 in the English, 16th of January, 1999. Your page 137. And it's for the 16th and you can see the block that surrounds it. All right? "Impact rifle brigades bring 22," and then "berets Beograd." "Berets Belgrade." What's all that about?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, a few moments ago I said to you this is my work notebook where I entered my personal obligations vis-a-vis superiors and vis-a-vis subordinates. So this is my work plan. This has to do with the list of officers and soldiers who will be in the organs that provide security on the state border. We had to know exactly who was where at what time. If somebody got killed, we'd have to know where this person was. Whether a soldier went out on mission, whether he got killed there, whether he came across a mine, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two words: "Berets, Belgrade," and we have got an eight-line answer that hasn't answered the question. Now will you tell me, please, what "berets, Belgrade" means. Does it mean Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Berets, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Beograd.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, those are distinction marks. It has nothing to do with berets from Belgrade or any kind of berets, because, for a sign, you always take part of military equipment and for the second part of the sign you take the name of a town or a mountain. So a beret is part of a soldier's equipment, and Belgrade is the name of a town. So we took two words, as we usually do, with the same initial letter. I cannot say "Shotka Beograd [phoen]" because that wouldn't be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not understanding this, I'm afraid. A distinction mark for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, all armies of the world when they secure a camp, a barracks, military installations, use distinction code names that consist of one item of military equipment and the second part of that code name or distinction code uses the name of a town or a mountain. Those code names are used by guards to distinguish between one another, and the shift leader --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So which military installation does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a camp which was the location of the unit. The broader area of Damjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on rapidly. We see on page 100 -- 47 in the English, 164 in yours, which is still in -- actually, we'd better focus a little more on 164, and maybe the Chamber will want on this occasion to go to the original as well. At some stage. 164, the outline passage, refers to masks doesn't it? Those are gas masks, protective masks. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you read my work notebook carefully, look at the date, 15th March 1999. That was the hand-over, take-over of duty of the company commander. Those are items of equipment that I found in the storage at the moment of transition of duty between the old company commander and the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the equipment and ammunition that I found in the warehouse, in the depot. Look at the date, the 15th of March, and it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go on to your page --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the items were inventoried.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to your page 166 -- and I think the Chamber may want to see this in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, is this a different hand-over from the change you talked about in mid-February? This is a different --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I handed over my unit in mid-February. That means I spent one month in the battalion command and on leave. On the 15th of March, the transition of duty procedure started between the new and old company commanders, the person from whom I took over. On that occasion, you have to inventory all the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at page 166 in the original. It can even go on the overhead projector. No, don't worry about that because we haven't got two copies, but the Chamber may want to look at this. On the 24th of March of 1999 -- there's nothing in the English, we didn't get this translated. I might have done, but I overlooked it. But on the 24th of March of 1999, we can see a whole lot of preparation for an operation, can't we? Yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is the 24th of March, after we received orders from the battalion commander. On the basis of that order for anti-terrorist combat, I established a combat group and listed the equipment that they were taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we go over to page 168, we come to the 28th of March. So that there is no entry of yours, none, to cover the period 25th, -6th, and -7th, is there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the system of reporting within the unit, this personal contact with the commander because he wasn't far away from me physically, I informed him through the messenger and through communications. All that happened during the anti-terrorist action was in the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simple point: Simply no record. I hadn't yet suggested that you should have kept a record, although indeed we've heard from other witnesses that records should be kept on a daily basis, but still, there simply is no record in your hand of what you did. You've produced to this Court exhibits 3 -- in the Delic exhibits, the number of which is 1 -- I don't have the number of Delic exhibits, but it's tabs 363, 388, 379, 411 -- 399 yes, Your Honour, I'm grateful; 399, 411 and 499, all of Exhibit D300.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 419. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've produced five statements setting out what you say is the detail of what you did on those days. Can you tell me, please, where the detail came from, since you made no record yourself?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all, I can't imagine how you can make notes during combat. There was no power, there were no basic items to enable that sort of work. We had to advance all the time to break up terrorists on our axis. We had no time for making notes. All reports were given to the battalion command, and on the basis of that, the battalion command made their reports to the superior command, and they kept a war diary. I, as a rule, do not write operation reports and do not keep a war diary, but it is my duty to inform the battalion command or battalion commander of everything that happened on my axis, which I did personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... remember when these statements were made, if they were made by you, to the VJ Commission for Cooperation in 2002?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the statements in person. Nobody suggested to me what to write and I don't know what other people wrote. What I wrote I wrote on the basis of what I remembered and what I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, when you wrote these statements it was all -- already three years and more after the event. You set out times, you set out trig points; all sorts of detailed events. We don't have time today to go through them in detail but the Chamber's alert to them. Where did you get all that detail from, Mr. Sel?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I not know it? I had the battalion commander's order. I received certain features, the axis for anti-terrorist combat, all the elements. Of course I know them. It doesn't fade from memory that easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So you can remember every detail now, can you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you last --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for combat actions, I can remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. You can remember the name of all the trig points that you went to, can you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line of taking up positions was on the Brod feature, trig 430, and in the evening I reported to trig 450 near Velika Hoca. Those features are etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the ones we have got etched in ours are 430 on 432, but maybe I'm getting it wrong. I'll come back to that if I have time. So you remembered these details, but can you help us yet with the name of the man Rambo? First name, rank, last name? Can you?
