If you can't, we'll go on to what you reported on the 28th of March, but before we do, just tell us this: You say you didn't have time to make notes. You spent a day in Mamusa, didn't you, waiting to right your upturned tank. You could have made notes then.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you listen to my testimony and read my statements, you know that I had two soldiers injured and one killed as well as that tank. My main idea was to save lives, transport these soldiers to the hospital and not to write novels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to the 28th of March, then, when, although you were still, I think, on the action, you recalled this - it's on the English page 48, halfway down - "Soldiers review, seize all technical goods and pile them up ... radios, caps and civilian items."

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 168 in your document, and it's the end of the blocked entry, and it reads: "Soldiers review, seize all technical goods and pile them up ..." Well, had your soldiers -- I don't wish to be too -- well, you just tell us where those technical goods came from if they aren't the product of looting. "Technical goods"; what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is the 28th March 1999 when I arrived with my unit in the area of Bistrazin. In the area of Bistrazin my unit was not alone. These are tasks given by battalion commander to me. That means that all units were duty-bound to conduct an inspection and to carry out these tasks. I didn't find anything on my soldiers, and I reported to that effect to the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if I understand this, seize all technical goods, but there were none, pile them up, but there were none to pile up. Is that what it amounts to? You had an expectation that they would have some looted property, but lo and behold, they didn't. Is that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm telling you again: This is one of the tasks received from the superior command. We had to conduct an inspection of the troops, and if we find anything, we had to assemble it in one place and turn it over, to avoid abuse. I didn't find anything on my soldiers, and I informed the battalion commander so. So that was one of the tasks within the anti-terrorist operation that was conducted in the place of rest. We had to inspect the troops and see if there had been any cases of robbery or looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 50 in the English, 175 in your version, please. And you're now disarming civilians, tying them up and handing them to the security organs. Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that written?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 175, in the block at the top right-hand corner, unless the translators have erred. There's the word "laundry," and then following the word "laundry" there's a reference to civilians. Perhaps you'd like to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as I said earlier, in that period the area of defence of my unit was attacked by a terrorist group from Korenica area. So in case we encounter any armed civilians, we were supposed to disarm them, because an armed civilian would not be allowed to move about the area of defence of my unit, and I had to provide combat security for my unit. So no civilians, regardless of whether they were Serbs or Albanians, could not walk about armed in the area of defence of the unit. So if we came across any such civilians, we were supposed to disarm them, tie them, and turn them over to the appropriate authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find any and tie them up?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Apart from the terrorist group that attacked me and, after a short struggle, withdrew in the same direction from which they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 178 in your documents, please, page 52 in the English. Have a look at that. Here's something interesting: You see underneath the listing of numbers of officers, non-commissioned officers and soldiers, "Check for the rank of the officer from Krajina," and then something, and then "Republika Srpska." Were you being reinforced at this time by forces from outside?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice, those are not troops. The commanding officer who was in my unit in that border unit, he asked me, because he had completed his school and later transferred to the army of Yugoslavia, his status had not been quite regulated, and he hadn't yet received any reply to his query about his rank, and the rest refers to the strength of the unit in that area, the unit under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the Republika Srpska? There's one from the Krajina. Or is it the same or is it different?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said a moment ago; it was a commanding officer who had completed an appropriate school, and after his job in Republika Srpska, he transferred to the army of Yugoslavia, but the issue of his rank was not settled. And through me, because I was his superior, he requested that his rank be recognised. That's nothing strange about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back to page 178. Go to page 179. What about the Russians and their visas? And then a reference to involvement of volunteers from the RS. Perhaps again you'd better read the phrase out. You see the little block there? Read out the first thing: "Question Russian visas." What does it say to you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That concerns the members who came of their own accord to the unit as volunteers. All of them were placed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of what? Where were the Russians coming from? You're saying individual Russians came down, did they, to join your unit?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there when I came, and they raised the issue of their visas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted their visas settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had four of them in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long had they been in your unit?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime until May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they left after a relatively short time. I didn't know their names because they were in the border unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So when they came --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- under the command of a different commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They came in May of 1999. How were they able to get into Kosovo to come and fight in May of 1999 when the NATO [inaudible] was well under way? Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there in the area when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, as tourists?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not me who brought them, they were in the border unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... well, who did bring them? Because other countries' forces fighting in a particular battle is something that's likely to be recorded somewhere. How did the Russian soldiers, if that's what they were -- were they soldiers or were they tourists who chose to become tourists?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not tourists and they're not what you think you were, nor were they army members. It's just that they felt it was their duty to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found them there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I don't know because they spent a very short time in my unit. I came to that area on the 27th of April. They were already there in the area, and they left in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the English, the date is incorrect. It should be 27th of April. And what about the next line but one. Just read that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next line but one after Russians, what does that say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Military service books." That means that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... next line.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- those soldiers who lost their service books -- activating volunteers from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That does look like a little bit like you've got volunteers from Republika Srpska despite your earlier answer. It's a little hard to read, "activating volunteers from the Republika Srpska" as anything other than meaning activating volunteers from the Republika Srpska, isn't it? So what did you do to activate these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, during the NATO aggression against our country, lots of people felt it was their duty to come and defend the country against the NATO aggression, and that's one of the issues that was raised when I arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what to do with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to page 178. Still on page 52. Village of Bob. Well, we know where Bob is; we've seen that. I've lost my map. It's not here. But you just tell us what is meant by "elderly woman slaughtered, man thrown to the well"?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is a report from my patrol that was kept contact with my right neighbour, which was the territorial detachment from Djakovica. According to the information they gave me, they had found those two bodies in the well. I wrote that down to report it to the battalion command. As far as I know, the battalion command sent a forensic team and military police to the site, to the location, and they found nothing from what I read from their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Soldiers reported on an old woman being slaughtered, or an elderly woman being slaughtered and a man thrown down the well, and nothing was found by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the soldiers who found them. There was the leader of the patrol, which was a commanding officer, and it was his duty to make a report after making contact with his right neighbour. He reported what he heard, and I reported it to the battalion command. The battalion command sent an appropriate team, an authorised team to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the end of April of 1999, the majority of the slaughtering may have already been done, and it may have already been obvious to you that the battle with NATO wasn't going to be won. Would that be accurate? The first part, the majority of killing had perhaps been done already. Right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have to repeat something that I've already said many times: On the 5th of April, when I arrived in that area and took up positions to secure the state border, there was not a single civilian in my area. That's one. Second, I don't do killings of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a murderer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nor do your troops.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither I nor my troops, and I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that by the end of April it was known that the battle was lost? That's one of the reasons, I must suggest to you, that the Obilic electric plant was being used to burn and destroy evidence of the bodies, but is it right that by the end of April it was known that the battle was going to be lost?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battle was not lost. The battle was lost at the negotiating table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. It's not my job to know. I was an officer. I was waiting for NATO forces to start the ground invasion and then I would ask them how they --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- feel, but they didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please. 53 in the English, your page 180. Two points. You see the block that surrounds the passage in which we have an interest. Again Deva seems to be within your zone of interest at the moment, is that right? Just yes or no. The border area of Deva.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the watchtower Deva with its entire crew, the border soldiers, came under my command. That is former military post 7238/8. And the post and packages that came to that address was forwarded by me to the new address.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now go to the 30th of April and read out the first two entries. We look at them - the translation doesn't always reveal this - these have got two stars besides them, two asterisks in your own hand. Matters of great importance. Just tell us what they read, will you.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first two notes, the first has to do with engineering preparation of defence positions, shelters, and the accent is on the preparation of shelters and covers. The second note is related to destruction of alcohol, the consumption of which was strictly prohibited. Further on, because of NATO airstrikes the targeted also civilian targets resulting in a lot of destroyed and killed cattle. There was Catholic population there, and there were lots of pigs, there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- uncontrolled slaughtering of pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was there -- yes, we'll come to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suspect the first line of translation may need correction in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you please, Mr. Sel, just read the first line and we will correct the English because it wasn't what I was expecting when I'd seen an earlier draft. Can you just read, without comment, the first line, please.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: First line: "Shelters. Accent or focus on shelters." I don't know how it's translated in your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Zaklani" would be "slaughters," wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is incorrect, Mr. Nice. I'm telling you nicely what is written. "Shelters," or cover, "focus on cover." Because of NATO airstrikes, we had to prepare proper shelters and cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, would you please read without comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think any ambiguity in the first line is beyond resolution in the time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now will you please read, without comment, the entry beginning with "alcohol."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The difference is only in one letter between "zaklani" and "zakloni."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're hearing a comment from the interpreter. What's that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is only different letter between the two words "zaklani," "slaughtered," and "zakloni," "shelters."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you now please read, Mr. Sel, the second entry, beginning with the word "alcohol."

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Alcohol to be destroyed, pigs to be driven out, not to be slaughtered any more." That has to do with cattle -- livestock, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Assuming it is cattle and the word wasn't picked up in the translation, what were the people doing slaughtering cattle in any case?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there was no need to slaughter livestock because we had our regular supplies. But because of NATO airstrikes, a lot of livestock was killed, and you know that pigs eat anything, and some soldiers tried to pen in pigs and then slaughter them before holidays to eat them, but that was strictly prohibited to prevent infection and disease. So if any pigs were found, they had to be driven out and there was a prohibition on their slaughter. So the only thing that was allowed was to replenish supplies with meat from regular sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course with the Muslim community there aren't that many pigs kept for eating, are there, but --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, a moment ago I said that there was a Catholic population living there, too, and as opposed to the Albanian Muslims, they do keep pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, we've heard quite a lot of evidence that not only were people killed and their property looted but that their animals and livestock were slaughtered wantonly in the start of the campaign. Is that what you're referring to here, if this does indeed refer to cattle?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is an order by a superior command. So it was my duty as the unit commander in that area to review the units, to destroy any alcohol, if I find any, and to look after -- to look after the livestock, that if there were any intentions of slaughtering any cattle, to let them roam free and to prevent the slaughter of the cattle. Because we had regular supplies, food supplies coming in to us, so we didn't need to slaughter the cattle for meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suggest that's not what it means, you know what it means, and it has something to do with the acts of criminality that you were engaged in, Mr. Sel.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Nice. That's your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to consider, please, some observations made in the course of the Mancic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have transcripts of the hearings of the trial. Interesting themselves because, for the four accused the trial hearing occupies only 112 broadly typed pages, but of course there's always the investigative judge's contribution. For convenience, I ask that the Chamber may want to follow it themselves in the original without prejudice as to whether it's moved into evidence as an exhibit. Otherwise, I'll lay the pages on the overhead projector, and we have the parallel pages in B/C/S for the witness to follow, and I've got 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 -- a little more than seven entries I want him to consider. He doesn't need to have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the trial that happened in 2002, as I've already explained, of Mancic, Radojevic, Tesic and Sergei or Sergei, and the first entry on your page 16 reveals, doesn't it, how Tesic said that Radojevic and Mancic ordered him to do the killing of the civilians that lay at the heart of this case. You know about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is the area of responsibility of another unit so there's no need for you to give me those notes because, as I say, that unit was 20 kilometres away from my area and I don't know what they were doing. If they had indeed something or committed anything, then they should be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Kusnin murder occurred on the 11th of April. We've had sight of Vukovic's diary which says that on the 5th of April you were sent to Kukaj. Kukaj is in the same area as Kusnin, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Kusnin and Kukaj are about 20 kilometres away as the crow flies. Kukaj is near the Deva watchtower. Take a map and have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moreover Tesic, Sergei and Radojevic had all been under your command at the time when they entered into service in this area, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what I'm telling you is that you're not well versed in military matters. While I was responsible for the unit, where those units were under my command, that is to say until the 15th of February, I guarantee that they had not committed any crime or anything similar to that. Now, what happened when I left the area, I really don't know. So I state again, if something happened, then they would have been held responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 29 of the English and going over to page 30, what Tesic said was that they weren't told how to treat the two civilians apart from killing them, but he then said this - top of page 30, and it's highlighted for you on page 16 - "I did not hear about the existence of any Geneva Convention regarding protection in wartime. None of the officers ever told me anything about wartime treatment of non-combatants." So that covers, on any reckoning, your period as well as anybody else's. Tesic, the soldier for whom in due course Vukovic was going to go and give character evidence in support of him, never told about the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there's no mention of my name anywhere there, so as I say, this is quite useless because this happened in the area of responsibility of another unit. So I do not know what happened over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whatever the --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there's no need for me to discuss something that was -- didn't take place in the area of my responsibility, so I am responsible for the situation in my area of responsibility and my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right, then. You point us to the contemporaneous record of your briefing of your soldiers, including Tesic, where they were given a lecture about the Geneva Convention. Just tell us. Where can we find it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as I know, that is to say the professional organs would come to the unit and hold lectures about war law and the Geneva Conventions, they talked to the soldiers about them, and I said that each soldier had a separate booklet about the conduct of soldiers in combat, and so did all the commanders. They had the basic tenets of war law. They didn't go without that. So apart from being acquainted with it, they would have the brochure on them, with them, and at any rate everybody is responsible for their own conduct and behaviour. Now, I'd have to go through all my work --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- notebooks to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is something that, for example, your brother officer, Captain Rangelov, would know, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You'd have to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, you see, if you -- just for the --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly. And we've got some more entries to look at before we get to Rangelov, but since you make the point, be so good as to go to your page 26, and we'll go to our page 52 in the English. This is Rangelov speaking in court. And what he says is this: "After I received information about the event -" which is the killing at Kusnin from Lieutenant Radojevic - "I subsequently met Major Mancic in the presence of Lieutenant Radojevic. I told him this shouldn't happen any more, that I as a company commander wouldn't permit it. After that, I started including in my orders items about treating the civilian population, prisoners and wounded men in accordance with the Geneva Convention." Even your brother officers acknowledge to the Court that there was no pattern of instruction about the Geneva Convention. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I repeat again: I'm responsible for the area of responsibility of my unit, and I know quite distinctly that I informed all the soldiers about the measures and took all steps to prevent any untoward actions from taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go back to our page 30, your page 16, please. The only reason this crime was tried at all, as I must suggest to you, was because, as Tesic said, he first reported the event to the security organ officer in his unit, Officer Rudic. Did you know Rudic?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you understand that the bodies that were -- of the dead people, the dead men were subject of an unsatisfactory, incomplete fire? Did you understand that? If we go over to page -- sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I repeat again: This is the area of responsibility of another unit and what happened there is something I'm not aware of, so I can't tell you something I did not see or hear about. I only heard about it when the trial began, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, all these men were under your command or your associates. For example Kolundzic, we haven't taken the time to do it, his name is all over your diary. If we go to page 31, we see that Tesic explains the following -- top of the page. It's your page 17, please. Page 17. You've got the highlighted area. "Immediately after this event -" that's the following day - "Kolundzic reproached me for not setting fire when a fire should be set, and he mentioned The Hague." You officers had in your charge very young men and you could make them do what you wanted, and when any of them resisted, you could still threaten them with something like The Hague. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is certainly not the truth. So with my own personal example, I always influenced my soldiers and would never have allowed them to do anything that was not permitted. And let me state again, what happened in the area of responsibility of another unit is something that I am not interested in. Because everybody must hold responsibility and take responsibility for what happens in his own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tesic's own use of drugs, Your Honours, can be found on page 32, but for want of time I go to his co-accused Sergei's use of drugs, on our page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you go to page 21, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness had said for ten times that that has nothing to do with his unit at all and I don't know why you are permitting Mr. Nice to waste time in that way, and I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that his cross-examination has been going on now for at least three times the length of mine and he has not challenged a single portion yet of what the witness testified about in the examination-in-chief. He's dealing with matters that have nothing to do with the testimony and the examination-in-chief and at the same time things that have nothing to do with this witness either, and he is wasting time quite unreasonably so, so I don't think there's any point to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you had indicated you were bringing your cross-examination to an end. I will allow the question, Mr. Milosevic. It may be that it's a matter in respect of which the witness has some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, these young men were in your charge, under your command, at an earlier period of time. So let's look at your page 21, page 40 in the English, and remember what you said about drugs and alcohol. Now, this is what this young man said: "Before that evening, that event in the evening, I had taken Trodon, or Troedon [phoen]. I don't remember the quantity, and I'd mixed it with alcohol. I also took it after the event. The event took place in daytime at some point between 1000 and 1400 hours. I'd been taking narcotics before my military service, such as Trodon, marijuana, LSD, and ecstasy, and I smoke grass less frequently and in smaller quantities." Your men, in order to do these ghastly things you required of them, sometimes had to be on a combination of alcohol and/or drugs, didn't they, and you knew that.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's just not true. That is the statement of a witness aimed at defending his acts and what he did. This soldier Tesic, while he was in my unit, was my personal security, and I guarantee with my head on the block that he never used drugs or alcohol. Otherwise, I would have sent him packing had he tried to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so, because I didn't need a soldier like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quickly on to page 54, your page 27. Now, this is in the evidence of Rangelov again. This is what Rangelov said on -- parallel officer to you, page 27. He said: "I know that some soldiers took --" first of all, he says: "After the beginning of the aggression, I didn't organise any training regarding the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and I don't know whether the platoon commanders did." But he then says this: I know that some soldiers took various kinds of drugs and drank alcohol while carrying out tasks in Kosovo and that they mixed drugs and alcohol. I'm not aware of any deals with Tesic particularly." Even your brother officer knew that your soldiers had to take drugs to do what was required of them. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice that's just not true at all, not true at all. That is your observation and conclusion. I state again that while soldier Tesic was under my command, he didn't use any drugs or alcohol. Now, the fact that they gave statements of this kind, you can ask the Trial Chamber why they gave such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the chamber that they gave the statements to. And I know that in the area of responsibility of my unit, it was strictly prohibited to drink any alcohol or do anything else along those lines. So I didn't have any problems with that at all. It all depends on one's relationship to one's men and how you command your soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, you have asserted absolutely systematic instructions on the Geneva Conventions. Let's see what your superior officer, who has been a witness in this court, Vukovic, had to say about this on page 75, at your page 36. This is the high -- the high point, as far as he can go, and he says this: "During the above-mentioned aggression we did not have any particular training about how to treat the civilian population, wounded persons, prisoners. In this regard we had instructions which were kept by company commanders. These instructions set out how to treat these persons." Then he goes on to say the officers knew which -- which orders to obey and which not, but he makes it clear there was no particular training about the Geneva Conventions. There was none, was there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I am responsible for the situation in my unit and I know that my soldiers were aware of this and had what they had with them and on them. Colonel Vukovic came towards the end of July 1998 to the unit. Now, why his former commanding officer didn't inform him of things like that is something I really can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Sel, as a result of your coming here and as a result of your eventually providing or having provided for you a contemporaneous record, it's been possible to find people who actually served with you. Contrary to all the evidence you gave about not involving Bela Crkva and not being involved at Celine and doing nothing at Mamusa, the truth is that from 1998 until 1999 the army in Kosovo was acting without any regard for the law. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would you please limit yourself to my unit. As I said, I am responsible for the situation in my unit. I know that my soldiers, my subordinates did not commit any crimes or evil acts, and I stand behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you exercised the power of life and death, and so far as women were concerned, you exercised the power over whether they should be abused and violated or not.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I do apologise but I have to repeat yet again: You are persistently trying to put before me a statement of a unit who left five days after I had come to the unit. Nothing happened. No civilian murders, no rapes, nothing of that kind while I was in command of -- of my unit. So these are statements from soldiers who had fled from the unit and tried to be granted political asylum in some other country on the basis of their false statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not so far --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I've come here for the truth and I have taken the oath and declaration to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... appreciate Witness D was a soldier right to the end, and you've come here, Mr. Sel, to lie to this Court without any contemporaneous document to support either the statements you made to the VJ commission or the maps that were drawn by someone for you to adopt. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all, you've insulted me. I haven't come to lie here but to tell the truth, and it doesn't serve you in good stead to say that. I stand by what I said in my statements and my work. I'm a professional soldier. Let me repeat that once again. I conducted myself professionally. It is common knowledge against whom an army fights, launches into battle, and against whom it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last repeat question but I want you to have a very good opportunity to consider this. Can you, for your unit or for Vukovic's unit if you have the knowledge, can you point us to any document that shows the taking of a prisoner of war or even a prisoner in the 1998 period and shows us what happened to that prisoner? Can you point us to any document?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think that you should contact the former military court in Nis and the prosecutor there. That's where you'll be able to find the exact data about what was done to the terrorists captured in 1998. They were handed over to the proper authorities, to the military court, and were taken before that military court. There was no killing or any other crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ambushed, killed by you without regard. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I do entreat you not to present fabrications of that kind. That's pure fabrication. The army just carried out its assignment. The terrorists started arming themselves first, bringing in weapons and fighting the army and legal authorities. We didn't pick a fight with them, they started fighting us, and it would appear, would it, that our officers and soldiers died of their own accord and were killed by an unarmed people. That's what one can deduce from what you're saying. And the army never opened fire first. It always opened fire second, with the aim of defending itself and its lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how long will you be in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite obviously I have very little time left to the end of today's work. I'll try to use the time as best as possible, not to have to keep Lieutenant Colonel Sel here longer than today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We will adjourn for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should have asked for the notebook of the witness to be exhibited and I don't think I've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. It will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Transcript of the Mancic trial is a document of record provided to this Court. It's a matter entirely for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any observation with regard to the admission of the Trial Record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, the notebook and the translation of the notebook. We were very dissatisfied with the quality of the translation. Passages have been selected. For instance, the slaughtering passage. And on the face of it, it looks highly suspicious and incriminating evidence. Then you go to the passage itself in which apparently the B/C/S words used weren't clear in the Prosecution version, and they're quite plainly clear when you look at the original. The word "pigs" had been omitted, and that is a less than satisfactory way for the Prosecutor to operate within this courtroom whilst a witness is being questioned. We don't have time to check everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you're not attributing any ill motive to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it's less than satisfactory, and I would hesitate to go any further, but I think what should take place is that there's an official translation be produced of those passages that were used rather than the draft that we've got attached to it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Kay. In ideal circumstances, yes, we should have an official translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the transcript of the other proceedings, in our submission that is not admissible for the same reasons that the Trial Chamber has given on many occasions before concerning the statements of other people not being called as a witness, and it's not a document arising at the time, it's not a document that speaks for itself, and the content and material is plainly challenged. So that, we do not agree should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to express --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have to express the gravest concern about Mr. Kay's expressions of concern. In fact, they're really quite offensive to a group of people who have worked extremely hard over this weekend to provide the best possible translation in the shortest possible time in circumstances where this witness could reasonably have been expected to have come with contemporaneous material and to have it been translated either by the accused or perhaps by Mr. Kay, fulfilling his functions as assigned counsel. This material, it was first read once by an individual in my team and the shortest translations were done. It was then necessary to get extremely capable and industrious people to work over the weekend, which they did, and as I recall, the last part of the translation came to me by hand at about 5.00 last night. These people work extremely hard and it is actually deeply offensive for somebody who doesn't read the language to say the sort of things that Mr. Kay said, and I take exception on behalf of those members of this office who did this work. I deal with a particular example. You take the word for either "shelter" or "slaughter." The word, as it's read, looks as though it's an A not an O, to me, and it's the difference between an A and O that makes the difference. As to the omission of words that are not clearly legible, I've always given a chance to this witness to try and read them himself, and the Chamber will recollect that I expressed some concern about that line and got him to read it for us. So those remarks from Mr. Kay absolutely rejected and I stand by the staff who worked so hard to try and keep this Chamber adequately equipped with useful material. So far as the transcript of the trial is concerned, this is a document that in some Chambers I think would be regarded as self-producing, that is to say it's an official document of record and it's been provided to the Tribunal. It's plainly of value and it's plainly of value because if somebody says something under the equivalent of an oath in a court of the former Yugoslavia, although you'll discover that the various witnesses from the Prosecution and defence say different things, of course, and leads to a decision by that court which was to convict all four men and to sentence them to terms of imprisonment from, I think, 7 to 3 years, then the observations made in the course of that trial may be of value, particularly the observations about drugs and the Geneva Convention, and I'd invite the trial -- the Trial Chamber to consider admitting it because it will plainly be of value. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, as far as this document is concerned, about the trial that is, the trial of these four men referred to by Mr. Nice, I wish to remind you of the following: That Mr. Nice even said something inaccurate to the witness, that this was practically the only case when someone was brought to trial. That's not true. You saw General Gojovic's testimony where you saw that a large number of people were tried, even during the course of the war. Now, can this document be used as evidence is a different matter altogether, but it cannot be introduced during the testimony of this witness because this man has nothing to do with these men. It's not his unit. It would be as if you were to introduce some other document that had nothing whatsoever to do with his testimony. That is what I wanted to say on that score, but as far as the notebook is concerned, I fully agree that the work notebook should be exhibited but only in the original, not the translation. And you see that it is a translation with shortcomings, with some cardinal mistakes, and this is not the first time you've seen that, that there are such mistakes made in the translation. You've seen that there were many mistakes in the TV series that you had to check out here, only those that you did check out, let alone all the other ones where you did not check them out, and you yourself, Mr. Robinson, said several times to Mr. Nice that these were big-time mistakes. So I would not assume that Mr. Kay's comments were insulting to the translators or something like that. I think that that is rather an overstatement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The record of the trial will not be admitted, in accordance with our practice. The notebook, we'll admit those parts that have been referred to during cross-examination, because they have been -- those parts have been adequately translated. Any mistakes that were made have been corrected. And I'd like to say that the Chamber does appreciate the efforts of any party to have a translation done, because we know that the official translators are besieged, are under tremendous pressure. We note, however, that at times mistakes can be made, and when that is done then we have to take the necessary measures to have them corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And of course any parts of the notebook dealt with by the accused in re-examination will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be 938.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sel, Mr. Nice suggested to you that there were no arrests or captures. Do you know how many members of the KLA were amnestied after the 5th of October? They were pardoned and released from our prisons.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as far as I know, they were all set free, all of those who had been sentenced previously. I don't know exactly the numbers involved, but I know that practically all of them were let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, several hundred were released. Could they have been released had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and the question was not whether there were any captures, the question was whether this witness has come here with any knowledge of records or details, and the answer to that was none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I remind you you're not giving evidence and no leading questions. Let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he himself said that he knew that they were all released. Only those who had been arrested could have been released, not those who were killed, but all right. Let me try to deal with this, these questions. Please place on the ELMO this page 180, the one that was mistranslated, but please place the original on the overhead projector, so in the Serbian language in the witness's handwriting. I asked for the original to be placed, the original page so everyone can see what is written there. The handwriting is rather legible there. The page is 180.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where there are two asterisks, it says what? Read it out once again, and you can all see what it says here where the two asterisks are.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this was one of the main tasks in order to prevent losses from NATO attacks, that is to say shelters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down. The interpreters cannot keep up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Sel, the interpreter is asking you to slow down. Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the word "zakloni." It is used twice. In both words you have A and O, these two letters. Look at it: "Zakloni."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The correct interpretation is not for the accused, and he's doing what's done before with matters like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I agree entirely because the two As -- rather, the two that are supposed to be Os, one of them plainly looks like an A. It's there to be seen no matter what the accused might say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you take this any further?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in the English and in the Serbian language - and the script here is Latin - A and O is written the same way, so there's no need to interpret that or translate that. Could you please show the word "zakloni" and "zaklonima." The letter A is the second one and the letter O is the fifth one in these words. Can you not distinguish between the two? It says it there very nicely "zakloni" and "zaklonima."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I marked my text as being ambiguous, and I'm not going to take any points on it at the moment unless the accused insists because, for what it's worth, I don't read it in the way the accused is reading it, but there it is. But if the accused is simply going to destroy the value of any form of examination by repeatedly refusing to obey the Chamber's orders not to put words and letters into another person's mouth, why don't we just move on and doing something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you have a question to put to the witness, without yourself giving evidence, you can put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, what about the handwriting? Do the letters allow any dilemma? Is this not legible enough for you, and I hope for everyone who is watching this broadcast?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is no doubt about this. It says very clearly "zakloni" and "zaklonima." It is an evident difference between the letters A and O.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next two asterisks. All right, alcohol, destroy alcohol, and you said about that, and then after the comma what is the other word?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other word, Mr. Milosevic, is "prasici"; piglets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, piglets should what?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Piglets should be taken out and no longer slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Piglets, that's the word used; piglets.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sel, please, the question of ambushes was raised several times here. Is an ambush a legitimate and usual activity in providing security for the state border or is it just something that you ordered?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is a legitimate combat task that is carried out, not only for providing security on the state border but on all other areas as well. So it is a classical form of combat except that we applied it here on the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you placed these ambushes in-depth?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that if somebody comes across an ambush, he'd have to pass by the border security?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, until that moment, until a given moment, the army of Yugoslavia did not have the right to enter the border belt. It is well known who secures the state border. In-depth security means the first and the second lines. It is the border guards that are on the first line. So if something or someone passes by them, if they were not in a position to a cover this, then they come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that what can come to you is something that managed to slip by the border guards?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No one else could come across except someone like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is the duty involved then? What is the customary number of people involved in such an ambush?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, usually it would be ten to 12 men, including their commanding officer. So always soldiers were accompanied by their active-duty officer in charge. So on the basis of estimates made in terms of what groups would try to get through a given area. So it can also be more people that can be involved in an ambush. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that ambushes were placed in areas where smugglers were expected to pass through. You used that word "smugglers," armed smugglers.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. They -- these ambushes are placed where it is expected that armed smugglers will pass by; rather, armed terrorists coming in from training in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what would the task of the ambushes be? So the group would go by the border guards, they didn't notice them, so what was the task of your ambush, to shoot to kill or what? Tell me quite simply, what is the task of people on ambush duty?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, ambush duty, according to all the rules and regulations, is to issue a warning, first and foremost, to persons who had come. However, since it's a question of night-time, depending on the strength of the enemy, then they would be taken out to a given area. In this case, they were warned and they were the first ones to fire at us. Our people only returned fire if they would shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if they would shoot.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it always was. We were never the first to open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, how many times did it happen to your unit that they would open fire when they were in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, Mr. Milosevic, my unit, in addition to the everyday ambush duty that it was involved in, never opened fire because no one tried to pass through my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no such attempts in your area?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The question of Smonica was raised. You dealt with terrorists in Smonica; right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in 1998 that was one of the strongest terrorist strongholds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in that area -- that in that area 20 soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there were about 20 soldiers and officers killed, and some were wounded; some seriously, some less seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What killed these soldiers and officers in that area?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, they were killed from terrorist fire, by terrorist fire; fire coming from the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice suggested when you were talking about mortar support that you had at the time, that mortars were randomly firing at the village. Was there any random fire coming from the mortars?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, Mr. Milosevic. Our mortars never opened fire randomly, but they always did the appropriate calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the 120-millimetre mortar a precise weapon, the one that was mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hands of a good operator, a trained soldier, very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was fire ever opened randomly, not at a firing point?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no random fire ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice suggested that the bodies of the persons killed became a problem in April. Did you have anything to do with the bodies of the persons who were killed?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as I said, I never had anything to do with the bodies of killed persons because I never found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that they were successfully pulling them out.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said when I testified the last time over these past several days. They had a system pulling their wounded and dead out. That is to say, we found traces of blood as they were being dragged out, then also parts of uniforms soaked in blood, but we never found any wounded or killed terrorists, at least not where my unit operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 62 of the diary, or, rather, not the diary but the work notebook, the expression "arrest and tie" is used. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does "arrest" imply tying, that is to say handcuffing or using something else if you don't have handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is as common knowledge, the soldiers didn't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- don't answer that. Move on, Mr. Milosevic. You have destroyed the effectiveness of any answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were questioned at length, Lieutenant Colonel Sel, here with respect to the soldier that was -- that we called Soldier A here.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Soldier A is mentioned on page 33 of your notebook. Can you find that? Can you see that there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 25th of June, 1998. It says, "Search for (redacted) (redacted)."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then what does it say? "Check to see if he has arrived at the barracks."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're in open session. That shouldn't have been mentioned, so that's to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he wants to pursue the matter, it ought to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you -- are you going to pursue this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I won't mention names. I did say Soldier A. That was spontaneous in the quotation, but we can refer to him as Soldier A, not to have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, so far as Soldier A is concerned, after all the -- the prescribed five days, I had to check whether he had reached the barracks and, if not, that within the space -- the legally provided space of time a pursuit was launched, search was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say after he had been -- gone missing for five days?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to name -- Mr. Robinson, name names at all. There is no need to go into private session. I'm not going to mention any names, I'm referring to the person as Soldier A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, he's achieving exactly by relating back to something that was done last week. For anybody who wants to do it, he's achieving exactly the same result. If he wants to raise this matter now it has to be done in private session. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the statement to which reference is made?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this whole -- this should be in private session, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we only have 15 minutes. Where are you in your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite obviously I can't conduct the re-examination as I had envisaged to do because Mr. Nice quoted very many things, but I'll do my best to use at least those 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at page 31 now, please. Let's just go over certain matters but as quickly as possible, please. Have you found page 31?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say up there? Prevent what? Prohibit? It's in line 9. Prohibit what? Can you read that? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it says "Prevent looting and taking away of weapons or equipment from civilian houses."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's see what you refer to. Look at page 41 now, please. Have you found page 41?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say here? "To open fire," what?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Prepare weapons for going into effect at night. Open fire only when you have visible targets and when you see a flash."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And underneath that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to an order from the commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, on the 5th of July, there was an official discussion. What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 5th of July, 1998, at 2100 hours, an official interview was held with Branislav Kovacevic with respect to giving an official rifle to --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down because it's impossible to follow at that rate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Please slow down. The interpreter cannot follow you at that speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On the 5th of July, 1998 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've read that out. Go on. Go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At around 1930 hours, when the state flag was lowered, Avramovic and -- in front of the camp said that Avramovic was not allowed to shoot from a pistol. Avramovic took a pistol from Kovacevic and put a bullet and fired three shots into the air, three bullets into the air." So he fired three bullets into the air. Kovacevic's behaviour was not conducive to the conditions prevailing on the terrain, and he knew that he was not allowed to give official weapons to somebody else to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. That means that you were -- they had had a bet that this one man was not allowed to shoot and then the other one went ahead and shot.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my legal responsibility as their commanding officer. I was duty-bound to take down a statement and to send it to the battalion commander for further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This one said he shot because they'd had a bet but he didn't jeopardise anyone's life, so this kind of - what shall I call this? - act of indiscipline, you're making a whole report even if there were no casualties.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm duty-bound to do so, even if there were no casualties. It took place in the camp, so steps like this had to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now look at page 47. You insist upon that. And it's the 29th of July, 1998, where it says, "The discipline of the soldiers --"

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The discipline of the soldiers, they're too relaxed, that the -- discipline should be raised and that they should be properly dressed and look like soldiers, that they should be well and properly turned out like soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 58 now, please. What does it say there? It is the fifth line from the bottom. There is an asterisk. It says: "Prohibited contact with --" what does it say there, page 58? Forbidden contact with whom?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forbidden contact with civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Turn the page, and that's on page 60, the next page. What does it say at the bottom there, "Disciplinary measures --"?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Disciplinary matters should be discussed immediately or resolved immediately and steps taken against the soldiers that have upset law and order where they have failed to perform their basic duties."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, on page 65 what does it say there, somewhere in the middle? It says, "Undisciplined soldiers should be punished." Can you read that out.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says: "Undisciplined soldiers should be punished, that is to say prevent all forms of lack of discipline where law and order is upset and stimulating matters should be on a company level for soldiers who are carrying out their assignments properly."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say on page 116 now in the middle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can you go back to page 60, the line we read just now, "Disciplinary measures." The previous paragraph, what does it say, Mr. Sel? "Popovic, Misel, Kozarski." Could you tell me what it is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, this is what that it is about: It says: "Regular reporting to the battalion commander, rewards or penalty." So Srdjan Popovic, Sergei Misel, or Kozarski Darko might have stood to gain a reward, whereas disciplinary measures should be taken against soldiers who had done something wrong. So I can't remember whether they were stimulative measures or disciplinary measures; whether they had done something well and should have been rewarded or something bad and should have been sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at page 116 now, somewhere in the middle. It says, "opening fire."

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, three asterisks, the same thing: "Constant tasks, opening fire only at certain objectives." That means no random fire and no unnecessary opening of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you also describe some emergency event on 131, page 131.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bullet was fired --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down considerably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, you have to slow down considerably, considerably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. "Bullet fired at KPS3 guard post. All soldiers should be checked, and they should be told of the possible consequences as regards the security of other personnel."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you're writing down even the smallest omissions. On page 135, at the bottom, "Behaviour of soldiers." What else does it say here?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Behaviour of soldiers and soldierly appearance - without complete equipment they cannot go anywhere." I think that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And the next page, 147, you say at the very beginning: "Draw the soldiers' attention to --"

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Draw soldiers' attention to wearing civilian clothing in camp." So it is impermissible to wear civilian clothing on camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at 168 and 169. You talk about the 28th of March, 1999. The first line, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first line, "Disciplined soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what does it say in the last three lines, and it pertains to the 29th of March, on this same page.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Review the soldiers' equipment once again. Transistors, Walkmans, cassette players." Since according to the rules they are not allowed to have that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please wait for the end. There is a passage omitted, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and the witness, because you are overlapping, we have just missed a passage in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It is prohibited to go to the store and drink alcohol. It is prohibited to leave the premises except if there is absolute necessity, inform soldiers --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for that. Look at the 1st of April. Number 2, it is prohibited to leave what? What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2, "It is prohibited to leave the camp. Children are not allowed to come near soldiers and also to get close to motor vehicles." That means that there were still civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And children were interested in motor vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as children usually are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What else does it say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Take away grenades, rockets, and other ammunition from soldiers. Vehicles should only be operated by soldiers, not -- only soldiers who are drivers, not officers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it's all --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say on the next page when you look at the next page, the top, after the list of soldiers, the caps, and what, prevent what?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 170, the very top. "Prevent --"

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's the next page after this one. Just turn the page. In the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The upper left-hand corner is the list of vehicles that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And below that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Prevent crime."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to see, what it says there. What is on page 172, what you wrote down there? "Warning to Serbian armed forces." What does it say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is one of the leaflets that came from NATO aircraft. There were several of them. I have them here. If necessary, I can read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But what does it say, what you wrote in your work notebook? You actually copied out a leaflet?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Warning to the Serb armed forces: You are at NATO's gunpoint. Stop your operations momentarily and return to your garrisons immediately. If you do not obey, NATO will consider -- continue attacking your unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we can't go beyond 1.43. There is another case here this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Just a few more questions. I'm going to put just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not a few more. I think just maybe one. Do you have just a few more to finish, to conclude your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be unfair to the witness if I kept him here any longer, Mr. Robinson. I would like to finish the re-examination today, so I really don't want to lose any time. And may I say that Mr. Nice, last time in public session, when quoting some statements, if I can put it that way, from his own transcript said many ugly things about the witness, and then in closed session you made it possible to me -- for me to say that this witness was lying, and that is why I want that statement to be struck from the record, because it is totally untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead with putting another one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's just see 182 and 183 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's here on 182, the third line from the bottom? The word "crime" is there, "kriminal." What does that pertain to?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help me find it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 182 at the bottom, the third line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It pertains to preventing all forms of crime in the area of defence of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What's on the next page, 183, on the right? "Sorties," and then what does it say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sorties by NATO Air Force, keeping communications, civilian population, thrust."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What was brought into question here was whether the soldiers were informed and whether training was conducted with regard to respecting international law of war. You showed the rules for combatants. Did every one of your soldiers have these rules?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, every one of my soldiers had these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did they get them?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was handed to them in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single soldier who did not receive a copy of these rules? Did they all carry them in this form that you have them here now, a laminated copy?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Milosevic, all of my soldiers had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously I cannot cover -- please look at this -- this other page after the counting. I haven't got the number here now. I think it is eight and nine.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the other notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What have you got here under number 1, 2, and 3, only three these things.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1, again sorties by NATO Air Force, communications, problems with the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does NATO Air Force have to do with problems with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why?
